content: Endometrial carcinoma is the most prevalent gynecologic malignancy globally, and it often develops through precursor stages of endometrial hyperplasia. Atypical endometrial hyperplasia represents a significant pre-malignant condition with a high likelihood of progression to endometrial carcinoma. This condition frequently affects younger women. Oral progestins have been employed as a conservative treatment option for young women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia. However, their use is often limited by poor tolerability and adverse effects, which can compromise their overall effectiveness. Consequently, there is a growing need to identify a fertility-preserving treatment that is both safe and effective, with improved tolerability and fewer side effects compared to currently available options. The levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) has been utilized to provide endometrial protection in women with breast cancer who are undergoing adjuvant tamoxifen therapy. Levonorgestrel exerts an antiproliferative effect on the endometrium, which is believed to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral and intrauterine progestogens in the treatment of atypical endometrial hyperplasia. A comprehensive search was conducted in July 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, to identify relevant trials. Additional searches were performed in November 2018 within the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility (CGF) Specialized Register and Embase. References from published studies were also reviewed, and ongoing trials were identified through five major clinical trial registries. The selection criteria included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing oral and intrauterine progestogens (LNG-IUS) against each other or placebo in women with a histologically confirmed diagnosis of simple or complex endometrial hyperplasia with atypia. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility of trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes of interest were the rate of regression and adverse effects, while secondary outcomes included the rate of recurrence and the proportion of women undergoing hysterectomy. The GRADE methodology was employed to assess the quality of the evidence. The review included one RCT involving 153 women, which compared the LNG-IUS delivering 20 micrograms of levonorgestrel per day with 10 milligrams of continuous or cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) for the treatment of any type of endometrial hyperplasia. Among these participants, only 19 women were histologically confirmed to have atypical complex hyperplasia prior to treatment. The quality of the evidence was rated as low or very low. Although the included study had a low risk of bias, the evidence was significantly limited by imprecision and indirectness. No RCTs were identified that compared LNG-IUS or oral progestogens with placebo in women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia. In the subgroup of 19 women with atypical complex hyperplasia, after six months of treatment, there was insufficient evidence to determine whether there was a difference in regression rates between the LNG-IUS group and the oral progesterone group (odds ratio [OR] 2.76, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.26 to 29.73; 1 RCT subgroup, 19 women, very low-quality evidence). The regression rate was 100% in the LNG-IUS group (6 out of 6 women) and 77% in the oral progesterone group (10 out of 13 women). In the overall study population of 153 women, the primary adverse effects observed during the six-month treatment period were nausea and vaginal bleeding. There was no evidence of a difference between the groups in the rate of nausea (OR 0.58, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.18; 1 RCT, 153 women, very low-quality evidence). However, vaginal bleeding was more frequently reported in the LNG-IUS group (OR 2.89, 95% CI 1.11 to 7.52; 1 RCT, 153 women, low-quality evidence). No other adverse effects were reported aside from nausea and vaginal bleeding. The authors concluded that no RCTs specifically focused on women with atypical endometrial hyperplasia were identified, and the findings were derived from a subgroup of 19 women within a larger RCT. All six women who received the LNG-IUS system achieved regression of atypical hyperplasia. However, there was insufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions regarding the relative efficacy of LNG-IUS compared to oral progesterone (MPA) in this subgroup. In the broader population of women with any type of endometrial hyperplasia, there was no clear evidence of a difference between LNG-IUS and oral progesterone (MPA) in the risk of nausea, but vaginal bleeding was more likely to occur in women using the LNG-IUS. Larger studies are needed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of oral and intrauterine progestogens in the treatment of atypical endometrial hyperplasia.
